title: Generation of large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity efficiency
authors: Simon K. Yung, Matthew S. Winnel, Timothy C. Ralph, Jie Zhao
abstract: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding has emerged as a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation with continuous variables. For photonic architectures, the major challenge is preparing high-quality resource states, which can be deterministically synthesised from many large-amplitude cat states. Thus far, only modest-sized optical cat states have been prepared experimentally, and the implemented methods are highly probabilistic. We propose an all-optical scheme utilising quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements to prepare large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability. Importantly, no particular photon-number outcome is postselected: all outcomes contribute to the accumulated photon number, with the protocol repeated until a required threshold is reached. We demonstrate that the scheme is robust to realistic levels of photon-loss, the dominant source of error in optical systems. Our results highlight the power of active Gaussian operations for state preparation and pave the way for efficient quantum error correction using bosonic codes.
summary: This paper presents an all-optical, iterative scheme to deterministically generate large-amplitude squeezed cat states, which are vital resource states for fault-tolerant quantum computation using the GKP code. By employing quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements, the method achieves near-unity preparation probability and remains robust against photon loss. This paves a more realistic path toward implementing bosonic quantum error correction in photonic systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is deterministically preparing large-amplitude squeezed cat states, which are crucial resource states for fault-tolerant quantum computation using the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code.
main_result: The authors propose an all-optical, iterative scheme that achieves the preparation of large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability and demonstrates robustness against realistic photon loss.
method: The scheme utilizes repeated quantum non-demolition (QND) interactions and photon-number measurements to amplify the initial cat state deterministically.
model_or_system: The work is situated in photonic quantum computation, focusing on generating cat states via iterative amplification loops involving QND interactions and photon-number resolving (PNR) detectors.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F$) of the output state relative to the ideal cat state, success probability ($P_{	ext{success}}$) of reaching a photon number threshold ($n_t$), and effective squeezing metrics for GKP breeding.
important_parameters: The number of amplification rounds ($N$), the level of photon loss ($\ell$), and the required squeezing level ($r$) are key parameters analyzed.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the feasibility of high-efficiency QND interactions and PNR detection, and models the process by tracing over measured modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the process flow, Wigner functions of the generated states, and comparative plots showing success probabilities and effective loss scaling for different amplification schemes.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first proposing the iterative QND amplification scheme, then deriving the fidelity and success probabilities analytically, and finally applying these results to quantify the required squeezing for GKP state preparation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck for continuous-variable quantum computing by providing a high-fidelity, scalable method for generating necessary resource states (cat states) in photonics.

In the first round, vacuum signal and ancilla modes are mixed via a QND interaction, after which the signal mode has its q-quadrature anti-squeezed. A measurement of n photons in the ancillary mode heralds an approximate cat state |C(√n, n)⟩at the output. The interaction can be repeated, using a new vacuum ancilla, to amplify the signal cat. After N rounds with ntot total detected photons, the final state approximates |C(√ntot, ntot)⟩, independent of the photon-numbers detected in each round.
